title: Recognizing a previously seen physical object
description: Tracking, visual re-identification, spatial context and episodic memory in wearable systems.

report.question: For a wearable egocentric-memory system, how can I determine whether an object observed now is the same physical object seen earlier after it disappears and later re-enters view? Compare approaches using tracking, visual embeddings/re-identification, spatial context, and episodic memory. Cite evidence for each recommendation
report.reasoning: For a wearable egocentric-memory system, determining whether an observed object is the same physical object seen earlier after re-entering view requires combining multiple complementary mechanisms. Tracking approaches like EgoSTARK maintain object tracklets even when hands leave the field of view by terminating only after 20 consecutive frames with a free hand. Visual re-identification employs DINOv2 visual features averaged over tracklet frames, matching them to stored instances via cosine similarity using a threshold of 0.6. Spatial context and object permanence reasoning are critical because visual-language models often fail by treating non-visibility as non-existence, incorrectly assuming objects leaving the camera field of view are absent rather than off-screen. Finally, episodic memory architectures and frameworks like VQLoC leverage shared DINO-pretrained ViT-B14 backbones and spatial cross-attention transformers to localize recent spatio-temporal occurrences of visual queries.
openQuestions: How can we minimize false re-identifications when multiple visually similar objects (e.g., identical coffee mugs) re-enter the camera's field of view in different locations?
What is the optimal balance between online tracking termination thresholds and long-horizon episodic graph retrieval to avoid state drift?

agents.name: Researcher A
agents.summary: To determine object identity after re-entry, systems utilize spatio-temporal tracking, visual re-identification embeddings, and structural frameworks like knowledge graphs and episodic memory. While DINOv2 visual features and spatial trackers handle short-term persistence, long-horizon scenarios benefit from episodic graphs that link recurring entities.

agents.name: Researcher B
agents.summary: Determining whether an observed object is the same physical object seen earlier relies on multiple complementary approaches. Visual embeddings and instance re-identification via backbones like DINOv2 or SWAG allow semantic-free appearance matching. Tracking-based methods leverage single-object trackers to follow objects out of view and maintain tracklets. Spatial context and episodic memory integrate temporal intervals, hand-object interactions, and structured knowledge graphs to resolve object continuity across long-horizon episodes.

agents.name: Contradiction Hunter
agents.summary: To determine whether an observed object is the same physical object seen earlier, systems can utilize spatio-temporal tracking, visual re-identification through feature embeddings, spatial context reasoning, or structured episodic memory. Empirical benchmarks show that pure appearance matching often fails when objects leave the field of view, highlighting the need for persistent state tracking and episodic grounding.

agents.name: Evidence Auditor
agents.summary: Existing video memory frameworks provide various mechanisms for tracking and retrieving objects over time, utilizing spatio-temporal tracking, visual re-identification embeddings, and structural memory representations. While VQLoC demonstrates high visual query localization performance using a shared backbone and attention, multimodal agents like WorldMM and AMEGO incorporate visual feature embeddings or knowledge graphs for object persistence. However, current benchmarks such as SAW-BENCH reveal that vision-language models still struggle with persistent object memory, frequently treating non-visibility as non-existence rather than maintaining a world state.
